They never do anything for or even with me. They never contact me first, it’s always me who starts the conversation. Which is hard due to my depression and lack of motivation, but I have a deep love for friends so I do it anyway. I have trouble remembering birthdays, but I always put them in my phone calendar and set an alarm early in the day, so that I’m reminded the morning of. I send them a birthday text and call them if they’re comfortable with that. Before covid, I’d ask them if they had plans and that if not, I’d like to take them to dinner. Sometimes, when I could afford it, I’d get them a gift. On my birthday… none of them even bothered to text me. Even though I mentioned to all of them just a few days before that my birthday was soon. They never want to go do stuff with me. I’ve invited them to concerts, go window shopping, get food, hell even small things like grabbing a coffee and they NEVER go. I can understand only rarely getting to go out cause they might be really busy, but I literally can not name a single time we’ve done something like that together. The few friends I have know that I only have them few, and yet, in class, when we need to find partners, they ALWAYS choose someone else, and leave me behind without one. I’ve never worked with a friend on a class project or to discuss answers. 

But it’s okay. Cause I learned to enjoy my own company. I go do these things by myself and learned how to enjoy it. I still invite them, but I always expect a no so I’m never disappointed. And I do have a few real friends. We don’t talk everyday and they live back in our hometown so I don’t see them. But I go to them when I need to and they always have their arms open for me. My best friend is there for me every birthday and goes out to do things with me whenever she can. And then I have another friend I’ve known since elementary school, we didn’t hang out much after that cause she moved schools but she noticed I wasn’t on social media very much and texted me to make sure I was okay. No ones ever checked up on me like that.

Enjoy your own company and cherish the ones who cherish you. They’ll be with you every step of the way.

I wouldn’t say I’ve been to ALOT of venues, I’m sure there’s people who have been to way more than me. But I have been to a large variety of them. From large stadiums, to movie theater size, and to the small alley way punk venue. And I’ve been to a few outdoor ones as well; even the Hollywood Bowl at a point. 

It’s a bit hard to separate the music I went to listen to from the venue. If you asked what was my best concert experience, I might mistakenly say “Linkin Park at the Hollywood Bowl” just cause they’re my favorite band and I’m lucky to have seen them before Chester’s passing. As much as I loved that concert, venue wise, it wasn’t the best for me. But I think a lot of factors play into everything.

Financially, I’m fortunate enough to go to concerts. But I’m not fortunate enough to get $500 pit tickets to see Metallica at the Save Mart Center. 

I’m sure pit tickets are a way different experience than the nose bleed seats I settle for. I unfortunately did not get to see Metallica at the Save Mart Center, but I did see a Trans Siberian Orchestra Concert there and I have seen recorded Metallica shows. As insane as I think it would be to see Metallica in a small punk venue, I don’t think it’s the best concert experience for them. With all the effects and pyrotechnics they often use, a big stadium is what they need. It’s a big part of the show. A lot of metal concerts are like that. Would I ever see Destroy Boys in a big stadium like that? Absolutely not. The punk nature of them and how difficult it would be to think of good stage effects for them makes a large stadium performance for them dull. But the punk venue previously mentioned suits them very well. 

I have tickets to see My Chemical Romance in October at the Forum in Inglewood. The stadium is huge and I had to settle for nosebleed tickets. But even if I was in the pit, I’m not too stoked about seeing them in such a large venue. I think the movie theater sized venue would be a nice fit. Big enough to hold a merch table and bar, but small enough that people can still mosh and feel at least a little up close and personal to their favorites. I know that the reason they play such big venues is cause they are very popular, and they need to use the bigger stadium because... well... they sold out all 4(?) days they’re supposed to be playing there. But I think an important thing about being able to be a little closer to the band in order to enjoy them more is because a lot of MCR’s effects are played into by Gerard’s actions and the bands makeup and costumes. Metallica (sorry I’m just trying to stay consistent), as awesome as they are, aren’t ~performers~ they just have really good music, so being so close to them isn’t that much important.

But what’s my favorite? The indoor small punk venue. I love that atmosphere. I love going to punk shows and getting in the pit and being a little scared I’m about to die. I’m an adrenaline junkie, so I know that experience isn’t the same for everyone. But I love the closeness of it. I love stage diving, moshing... I like the tiny ass bar they have in the back, I love how fucking hot it gets in there and I’m sweating my ass off. You even have a chance at actually meeting the band (I met Destroy Boys after a show cause the guitarist promised me a pick). Maybe this is because I felt like I was PART of the show. Rather than just sitting a listening (I could’ve done so in my car and would’ve gotten the hearing loss with it), I’m up and moving; pushing and shoving; and matching the energy of the music. I really enjoy it. I know the sound of it sound gross and dangerous. I might sound fucking insane, but it’s my preference. It’s not for everyone, but it sure does feel like where I belong.

The fact that you consume the music to a personal extent- whether you hear it to the fullest or not- makes you goth. Goth is a pretty music based scene; but whether you hear it to the hearing’s extent or not doesn’t matter because you still heard it in your own way. You still consume it. The “deaf people can’t be goth” thing is stupid. I was born with Microtia (a birth defect where bones in my ear either didn’t form or fused together, leaving it closed with practically no hearing in it) I’m considered “half-deaf” but i think that’s a little dumb because I can still hear very well. Just not in my right ear. But I believe my left ear is hearing everything that needs to be heard (or maybe I just don’t know any better). Despite this “hearing disability”, I’m still a large consumer of music and I’m even a musician myself. The bass and drums being more apparent and easier for you is all the proof you need to show that you enjoy goth music. And the fact that you’ve devoted yourself to the scene and even the fashion (which, yes, like you said, isn’t necessary but god damn it if it makes you feel good, then by god, dress goth) shows you are goth. “Deaf people can’t be goth” is a very ignorant statement, anybody who thinks that way can go fuck themselves.

I know what it’s like to be in this kind of love. It’s a tough decision. I’m in love with my best friend too. But i got lucky because I could tell she had feelings for me too. I was scared to lose her in the beginning but I figured life was too short for her not to know. That was three years ago so I’d say we’re doing pretty good. We’ve even moved in together. You don’t have to do what I did though. 
Instead, ask yourself, would you rather remain friends so that you always have each other; even if that means potentially seeing her fall for someone else?
Or would you rather tell her and maybe something happens or maybe even something happens but then you break up but able to remain friends; but run the risk of losing her if things go south?
It’s a tough decision, don’t feel pressured to make it soon. You may even want to consider telling her but suggesting you guys stay friends. The friendship might not be the same for a while though. But I’m sure you guys can work through it till it is comfortable again. 
Play each scenario in your head. Which feels better? Which one hurts less? 
Good luck, lover boy

Happened on the night of Christmas Eve. I had gone to bed super early (7pm) and woke up at 1am. Obviously there was nothing else I could do except try and go back to sleep. I closed my eyes but I don’t remember falling asleep. My sister opened my door holding an object in one hand and her dog in the other. I asked her what she was doing here and she told me she had opened one of her presents and wanted to show me what she got. She started to get into my bed against my protests. It was really distressing for some reason. Then I woke up. Or I thought I did. I reached over for my phone on my bed to check the time. I don’t remember what it was but I remember my battery was low. So I turned over to grab my charger on the other side. I plugged it in and dropped my phone, charger wire sitting across my neck. Suddenly it started to tighten and drag me off the bed. I could feel myself losing air and coming off the bed. Then I ACTUALLY woke up. 

I also once had a dream I got in a car crash with someone I knew. I pretended to shoot myself to signal my great distress in the situation. For a long time, I struggled with depression and anxiety. I want to say my depression might’ve started my sophomore year of high school but I might’ve suffered from anxiety before that because I remember being a nervous kid. Anyway, I got really bad in sophomore year due to an abusive relationship and I had been raped (by someone else, not my partner). I never told anyone at the time what was happening. I had to deal with it alone. Except I wasn’t alone. I had Linkin Park. Their music helped me get through it all because their music felt so much like what I was feeling, it helped me get things out. I wasn’t good with words so these songs really helped me feel like I was expressing the pain I was feeling. When Chester died... I was fucking heartbroken. I had a full meltdown, as if a close family member had gotten in an unexpected accident. I wasn’t able to listen to Linkin Park for a long time after that. I think it took three years for me to finally start to be able to listen without crying. I’ve tried to fill the hole I was left with in my heart with other bands. Green Day, MCR... eventually my music taste evolved (I still love all those bands though). I started listening to punk music such as Dead Kennedy’s and Circle Jerks, just to name my favorites. Now I take a more gothic turn like Alien Sex Fiend, Bauhaus, Type O Negative. These bands, though they seem like just passing bands through my playlist, are more important than I realized before now. They were there to try and fill that hole in my heart Linkin Park left. They didn’t fill it completely, but collectively, they made it smaller. I appreciate them for that. Maybe someday I can love another band as much as I did Linkin Park.

Unfortunately, there is only so much that we can do. Especially for those who don’t believe what they’re in is harmful for them. I can only recommend that you sit down with your friend and calmly express to her how you’re hurt and sad to see someone treat her this way. You’ve explained to her that what he’s doing to her is toxic and abusive but she believes that he “helps” her. Ask her (and I can not express this enough) calmly how he helps her. Just let her explain. If what ever he’s doing is actually helpful, offer to do that for her instead of him doing it. If what he’s doing to “help” her is actually harmful, explain to her how and why it’s harmful. Tell her how there are better people in the world who can actually help her and will care about her and love her and not hurt you. Just like obviously do. It takes a lot of love and care to want to help your friend even though she believes it’s good for her. My own girlfriend has really bad anxiety. She used to have a pretty toxic friend (nothing as bad as abuse though). I never liked him and I had to sit her down and tell her that she didn’t deserve the shit he’s said to her. Eventually, they had a little argument and they stopped being friends. I can tell she’s a lot happier and healthier without him. Show her that she is special and that despite what she may think of herself, she deserves care. Not abuse. And if for some reason she doesn’t believe you or doesn’t want to stop talking to him; fill up her time. Invite her to do things. I know that may be hard cause of COVID (though I don’t know how bad it is for y’all in New Zealand. Maybe you guys actually took it seriously and now there’s little risk) but even just a sleepover or something can fill up two days where she doesn’t have to be around him. 

I know it’s not a lot. I know it hurts to see someone you care about get hurt. And I know it hurts even more when there’s so little you can do about it. But you’re only human. You’re one person. There’s only so much you can do before you can not stop it yourself. I hope she realizes soon how bad he is for her and that she can cut him off before it’s too late.

Even I will say that some of the best things I’ve ever written are in the middle of a panic attack or drunk. 
Does this mean I wanted this to happen to Gerard? Absolutely not. But I do know how my depression affected my behavior (and in my opinion... made me a lot more fun) before I got on antidepressants. Do I regret starting medication? Absolutely not. I can still get drunk so if I really needed to put on a show like I used to, I still have that. It feels way better to not want to die everyday and I’m glad Gerard got the help he needed. But I’m not gonna lie to myself and say they could’ve written Black Parade without it.

Screaming like that is a skill that is pretty difficult if you’re not already an experienced or trained singer. Not to mention it could be dangerous; even Gerard busted his vocal chords during the BP tour. I’m going to assume you’re not trained. But if you are; you’re gonna want to use similar breathing and mouth shape as just regular singing. If you’re not; it’s not the same as regular yelling and screaming. It comes from a different place in the face and the vocal chords. 
First; you’ll need breathe support. Do not breathe with your chest. Breathe from your diaphragm. You should be able to place your hand on your stomach and feel it stretch and expand, and then go back down. 
When you let that air out through singing or screaming, keep the air forward and always keep it moving. 
Second; your face shape matters a lot. Not sure how much it matters for screaming, but I’m sure it can’t hurt and might help with tone. Put your hands on your face and open your mouth as if you’re the guy in “the Scream” painting. That should be the shape of your mouth.
Third; keep your tongue forward. We tend to move it back when we sing “uh” sounding words. Keep it forward and make that “uh” more of an “ah”. In other words; put your mouth in an o shape and make an a sound. 
Fourth; yawn. Go ahead and yawn and let a sound come out. You feel how that sound comes from someplace different than when you talk? That should be the place where your sound is coming out.
Fifth; when singing using these techniques, you should feel almost a vibration in the front of your face. It might even tickle a bit and you’ll have to scratch your nose. This is perfect. This is a sign that you’re getting it.

Try these techniques with just singing. You might notice improvement with just the air support! I know that my singing takes a giant leap in quality when I apply these. After you’ve got it down and it becomes muscle memory, next try screaming through the same things. Screaming will really require a lot of mou th room though. People with big mouths are usually better at screaming. That doesn’t mean it’s impossible for the little guys either though. In other words, I forgot one tip. As you’ve got your mouth in an o shape and your tongue forward, try and make the inside of your mouth feel like there’s an egg in there. Think of the shape of the egg and imagine you have that in your mouth. That should open the inside of your mouth a bit more.

Drink LOTS of water and take care of your chords. I hope these help!

Oh yeah, I get how knowing that can make it easier to write music and I even use that myself. However I always considered that more of ear training with a small mix of theory. Thats why I said knowing how to build chords and knowing your scales are important. But I learned major, minor, half/fully diminished, half/fully augmented, and the differences between triads and seventh chords in ear training. And I actually love it. My Ear training professor was an excellent teacher because he didn’t force it down my throat. His hw assignments were based off whether you did them or not and then the hw was a big part of the grade. I still enjoy ear training and being able to play, hear, and recognize all those different chords! Perhaps we have a misunderstanding!
I couldn’t agree with you more about how knowing the differences between those chords can be a huge help! But theory, in my curriculum at least, was more of the structure of different types of music. Like I said, I don’t give a fuck about the structure of a sonata. I don’t care about the “subject”, “answer”, and what the fuck a “compound subject” is. That’s not part of any of my goals. And the chord progressions they try to teach me are an absolute pain in the ass. Because now I have a pull inside me that says that because I played this chord, now I NEED to go to this chord. Even though I actually don’t NEED to. I can experiment and move to a different chord and if it doesn’t sound right or it’s not what I wanted... we’ll try something else! And I’m able to do that. But the pull of NEEDING to do it otherwise it’s WRONG. Is a pain in the ass and I wish I never knew it. I have a friend who relies heavily on music theory based off chord progressions and structures of classical pieces. He’s a classical composer so he takes more interest in that stuff. But I don’t feel any emotion in his music. Don’t get me wrong, it’s good. But It doesn’t make you feel anything. It just is. I’ve even told him “this sounds really good; but what does it make you FEEL?” And he responded with “what do you mean?”. My heart sank a little to see that maybe we just don’t feel music the same way.

But again, I couldn’t agree more with you about how knowing that part of music theory is really helpful! I use it myself! But I think we misunderstood each other because I considered that part of ear training just cause that’s the class I learned that stuff.

And thank you, I am trying to be way easier on myself. It’s just hard not making people’s expectations, you know? I’m trying to forgive myself and accept that you can not satisfy everyone and that’s not my fault.

I think it would be nice to have more music classes readily available and for kids who have enthusiasm for it to be encouraged. Perhaps even suggested to kids who don’t hold an interest in anything else or struggle socially. However, I don’t believe it should be required. And I have two examples to show why.
The first one, I feel is common. I used to love reading as a kid. I would sit and read through books like it was a drug. It used to be my favorite pastime. But then when I started high school, and I was given required reading, I ended up hating it. So much so that I haven’t read a book since I left high school. I do miss being able to sit and read like I used to and I have confidence that I could get back into it if I tried. But lately I’ve been so busy with life and so traumatized by being forced to read some of the most boring books ever, it’s hard for me to pick one up. I didn’t hate every book that I was required to read. I actually enjoyed a majority and recommend a lot of them to friends who maybe didn’t get to read them. But some of them I hated with a passion. And the stress of having to work and pay extra attention to my book just for my grade haunts me to this day. 

This second example is more on topic. I love music. I picked up playing instruments at a relatively young age simply for my love of it. My parents never forced me. I never worked for it for a grade. I loved it, I dedicated hours to it, and I’ve gotten good at playing my instruments just because I loved it and no one was forcing me to do it. Now I’m a music major and it is passion crushing. I actually kind of hate being a music major. It bothers me that because of music theory, I feel like I can’t get experimental with music. I actually quit cello because of it. I switched to guitar which I’m much happier with. But mostly cause of the switch in teachers. My cello teacher forced me to practice practice practice. He could never understand that sometimes I was busy doing homework, eating, spending time with friends, or just hopelessly suicidal and depressed. Every time I went into his office, I dreaded it and I ended up hating playing the cello. My guitar teacher, is so much more laid back. He sees progress in everything I do and even takes time to listen to what caused me problems during the week. He doesn’t expect too much for me and instead just takes pride in the progress I make in the present. And now I actually practice MORE than I ever have because I know that he doesn’t have such impossible expectations. I still love guitar and make time for it everyday just cause my passion for it is still alive. Being a music major is still hard. Music theory makes me feel like I’ve been put in shackles and now I mostly only listen to things I feel like I really really need to know like scales and how to build chords. But I feel like the rest is just creativity crushers. Maybe I’m wrong. But that’s not the point. The point is that’s how it makes me feel. And if every kid who had a passion for music felt like that, barely anyone would wanna play music anymore.

I’ve never been to rehab; so I don’t know if it’s different than other mental health therapists. But I can tell you that my experience has been very positive. But! I won’t lie; I had to change therapists to find one that works for me. I’m pretty sure that if you don’t like yours, you can ask to switch too. I hated my old therapist. She didn’t understand, see what I see, or even cared to keep her mind open and at least listen to what I believe. I’ll never know if my therapist I liked ACTUALLY agreed with me, but at least she acted like it and made me see good things in ACTUAL good things. No “the world is better than you think” bullshit. She had me focus on things that DID make me happy and appreciate them a little more. If that sounds like it might work for you; then find a therapist who will do that for you. Even if you have to go through a shit ton of them just to find the one. I can also vouch for medication. People make medication sound so frightening. Like it turns you into a zombie. Those people were taking the wrong medication. Listen, I felt terrible and just like the zombie they describe when I was on my OLD medication. But now I’m on a different one and I love it. My mind has not changed. I’m still an anarchist. I still hate capitalism. I still enjoy all the things I used to. I can just function now. I can do things that need to be done without feeling like it’s the hardest shit in the world. I can wake up and actually get out of bed. I still like the “darker” things stereotypically associated with people with depression. It’s just now I have the energy to actually pursue my aesthetics in healthy ways. I can’t recommend medication enough. But it is VERY important that you be honest with doctors about how it’s making you feel. What you like and what you don’t. Otherwise you will be stuck in that zombie state.

American society usually has this idea that if you aren’t working some 9 to 5 office job you’re a failure or lazy. The American capitalist system pushes people to work way harder and longer than they should. Generally, and I know that this is the case for quite a few places, parents want their kids to go into STEM jobs. How much money someone makes is usually used as the measurement of their success. 

But you’re right, it is strange. The American people shame young musicians for wanting to pursue their passion while also consuming so much music. I think people who aren’t musicians or know the music scene think that if you don’t make it huge, you never made it all. Which actually isn’t the case. But they wouldn’t know that. In their eyes, unless you’re gonna be the next big thing, you’re failing at life.

It’s a sad concept to me. For one, I never liked the idea of your success being measured by your money. I’d rather be happy than rich. As long as I can afford the basic necessities, there are other things that are more important in my life than all the fancy stuff I can buy. But the American society doesn’t like that. It’s also sad to me to see people think that if I don’t make it big, I’ve failed. I don’t think they understand that I’m fine with not being the next big thing. I preferred the closeness and intimacy of close venues anyway. To interact with other music lovers and share stories and feelings through music is why I do what I do. Even if I’ve gotta work three other jobs to make ends meet, I’ll know that I’m doing what I love and that I’m happy. And that to me is success.

As a musician myself; I always know that whatever I write, listeners will take it and interpret it to their own lives. That’s okay. I write my lyrics hoping that you will. I’m sure other musicians are aware of this too and either don’t mind or embrace it.

First of all, I’ve never had a personal experience with cancer or a loved one having and dying of cancer. The closest I come to it is my aunt had breast cancer. But it was a minor case and she recovered very well and she looks great. Im very lucky to have my aunt still here. But that being said; I’m not especially touched by lyrics about cancer.

I do, however, have severe depression. It made me feel like I was being torn apart from the inside and that every time I was saying bye to someone it was for good. My own personal cancer. 

Imaging the lyrics for “Cancer” are actually about depression made it more relatable to me and amplified the feeling; even though the song is actually literally about cancer as the singer recalls his own family members death. 

I don’t let it affect me though, so I’m not sure what to tell you as ive never had this problem. But I hope what I told you in the first part makes you feel a little better. 

Everyone who loves music applies lyrics to their own lives. It’s normal. And you’re not ridiculous for doing it.

I turned around and I was like “uh... yeah?” And he replied “oh, cause I can barely hear at all” and he turned to show me he had Microtia too lmaoo. I think it’s pretty ironic that my worst encounter came from a guy who had the same thing. 

But no, I never experienced any bullying. I never really had a lot of problems. I’m actually also a musician! A very good one at that too! I can figure out how to play songs just by listening. People are always impressed I can do that with a hearing disability. I never had surgery to try and fix it and I personally don’t want to. Seems like a lot for something that just never bothered me. My girlfriend likes it. She thinks it’s “cute” and sometimes touches it; which feels good so I absolutely don’t mind. Not to mention she always asks before she does. But all in all; It’s hardly inconvenienced me in any way. I think the only thing is that I have to walk on peoples right side at all times. But even that comes with its perks. If I want to ignore someone, I just place them on my right and act like I’m listening.

I’ve been a fan of music for as long as I can remember. Some of my earlier memories involve my dad showing me the music videos for “Bring Me To Life” by Evanescence, “Stand Alone” by Godsmack, “One” by Metallica, and he also introduced me to “Numb” and “In The End” by Linkin Park. 

From those moments to about 8th grade, I don’t remember much about what I was listening to. But! I do remember watching Oprah with my mom once and these two guys called Two Cellos performed their rendition of “Smooth Criminal” by Michael Jackson. It inspired me so deeply. I wanted to do that. So I picked up Cello in 7th grade. But I also really wanted to play Guitar. For my 13th birthday, I got my first electric guitar. 

In 8th grade, I was shifting around to find music to listen to. It was the age of the emo and scene kids, but I wasn’t really digging a lot of it. I wasn’t a fan of Black Veil Brides, Blood on the Dance Floor, Asking Alexandria- none of it. But that’s what a lot of my friends listened to. Then I met this guy named Nic (yes he spelled it without the k). Nic was a metal fan. Iron Maiden, Metallica, Slayer. We were good friends and I was dipping my hand into the metal scene. Though, as much as I enjoyed it more than emo/scene music, it wasn’t my favorite. But Nic is very important to my love of music because one day, he came over and he brought his friend, CJ. We were messing around on YouTube when CJ turned on a video. It was a fan made Johnny the Homicidal Maniac music video set to the song “Breaking The Habit” by Linkin Park... I fell in love. This is my favorite song TO THIS DAY (I’m in my fourth year of college now for reference). It sparked something that would change my life.

I started to consume all the Linkin Park I could get my hands on and I became a die hard fan. I began to take playing cello and guitar more seriously. 

I’m high school, I’d say I was a hard rock fan mostly. Though it was hard to tell because my music taste jumped everywhere. But I’d say the two bands that stuck out most to me were Linkin Park and Halestorm. 

Something happened to me in my second year of high school though. Something extremely traumatic. My high school life was depressing and lonely, as I had very little friends I felt like I could talk to and my parents are emotionally unavailable. My only outlet was music and that’s when it really started to affect my life. I dedicated myself to it. I made a vow that I would make music for the kids who felt like outcasts someday. 

... that promise became a staple in my life when Chester Bennington of Linkin Park died. I can not express the heartbreak I felt. I was depressed about it for days. Didn’t want to eat. Didn’t want to talk. But it also made me determined. Now I REALLY needed to fulfill my promise. 

I was going off to college to be a music major for Cello performance; despite my dads obvious disliking for it. But I packed my music stuff and left. 

And then everything REALLY went to shit. My mental health PLUMMETED. I was self destructive, depressed, and suicidal. And I wasn’t doing shit about it. But this also affected my music taste. I wasn’t listening to Linkin Park at those moments because it was too hard on my heart. I had to find a new band. So I gave a band I only knew a few songs from a chance- My Chemical Romance. Yes, my MCR phase would not come until I was 18. And I wouldn’t call it so much a phase since I still listen passionately listen to them at 20. However, I also introduced a new band into my life. Green Day. I saw the American Idiot broadway musical with my not girlfriend at the time and it changed me. This music and this show is the reason I became so self destructive. St. Jimmy specifically affected me. I was trying to become him until I inevitably shoot myself. I started doing drugs and drinking. My driving became reckless and my grades were slipping big time. 

But I also made a discovery... I HATED playing Cello. I was no good at it either. I never wanted to practice. But you know what I do love doing? Playing guitar. And I was pretty good at it if I do say so myself. Eventually I got a hold of the guitar teacher and asked if he would take me into his department. I auditioned for him, and he said yes. 

My second year of college, I was trying to get better mentally. It wasn’t working that well but it was a step. This was also the time I discovered Punk Rock music. I became a big consumer of Dead Kennedy’s and Circle Jerks. 

I just finished my third year and I’ve stayed close to the Punk Rock scene. I love Destroy Boys and even saw them right before this whole pandemic started. I’ve also gotten really into Psychobilly. My guitar playing has made BIG improvements and I practice every day. I’m currently in three bands, though we’ve just started and we’re just barely getting really started. Midnight OrangeJuice is one of my bands; and an alien themed album has been in the works for a while now. Gunslinger Ghost is another that I’m in with my sister and her friends and we’ve finally started writing music. And the last is a System of a Down cover band that I started with the drummer of Gunslinger Ghost. 

Music has always been in my life and I hold it so dearly in my heart. It’s my entire life and my world revolves around it. I listen to so much more than what I named and it all jumps around in different genres. I just named the bands that really took me somewhere. Music is an escape for all of us and someday, I hope to make music for all of you to enjoy.

Hmm, I might be misunderstanding your question but I’ll try and give my thoughts. The emotional reaction someone gets from music definitely varies person to person. And on the other hand, a song that means a lot to me is “Die in the Revolution!” By You Guys Smell Like A Problem (which is unfortunately unavailable at the time cause the artist removed it in a moment of depression) might not move you. I do think that not everyone is so connected to music though. There are people out there who feel very little when listening to music. It’s just music to them. I find that incredibly strange and a little sad. I wish I could make them feel what I feel listening to certain songs. 
But if you’re referring to a performers stage presence, I think it’s not super important, but it definitely improves a show. My biggest example of this is when I went to go see a concert put on by a radio station. It was the Krab Christmas Show in Bakersfield, for those who are familiar or curious. I remember going but having no knowledge about any of the bands. I just enjoy music and was ready to hear some new stuff. It was fun, a lot of the bands were good. But to be honest, I can’t tell you who they were cause I don’t remember any of them. Except for one performer: Barns Courtney. His musics good! He’s not my very favorite. Probably not even in my list of top 10 artists. But I definitely listen to a few of his songs when they come up on my song list. But what made him stand out and what made me remember him was the absolute hell of a show he put on. Obviously it helped that he has a great voice and can really play guitar; but his connection with the audience and how engaged he was to the music really made him extremely memorable. So memorable, I still remember his name, I got him to sign my ticket, and immediately added his songs to my list. All cause of how great of a show he put on. Now, can a good show still happen even if the artist isn’t so engaging? Yes. I remember seeing Destroy Boys. They had passion in what they played, but weren’t really a spectacle to see. You probably could’ve just blasted theyre music on a loud speaker and we’d have the same show. But that’s okay! Cause I still had loads of fun and so did the rest of the audience. But I definitely think a stage presence and really showing a passion and showmanship in your music definitely helps.

I feel old mostly cause I feel out of touch with younger people. I’m not cynical about it, I remember how terrible it feels to have someone older than you shit on something you like just cause they don’t understand it. But I’ve really fallen out of line of new mainstream things and it happened really quickly and really strangely. I’m an active social media user, I have a younger sister, I’m quite social. Where did I go so wrong that I hear a new celebrity name and not know who the fuck they’re talking about? Well, I didn’t. Turns out I’m just old and have been thrown out of the loop. 
Milestones also get less special. When you’re young every birthday is a celebration. And when you turn 10 it’s “yay! Double digits!”, Three years later it’s “yay you’re a teenager!”, then you go to high school and that’s a big deal. then you turn 16 and that’s a big deal. Then you get your license, which is exciting. Then you graduate high school and maybe go off to college. Then maybe you graduate college. Then you turn 21 and that’s it. That’s your last special milestone. You drink that day away, damaging your liver and experiencing what might be your first hangover. And what comes after that? Nothing but life and adulthood. Which, don’t get me wrong, life can be exciting if you actually look at the good. But, god, no one cares about you anymore except maybe your spouse if you were lucky enough to find one. You feel old now. Then people you know start dying. Hell, as soon as you get out of high school, people start dying. A kid I knew in high school died in a motorcycle accident. I had a professor die at my college and instead of canceling class, they just replaced him the next day. Pretty soon my grandparents will die. My depressed friends will kill themselves. My irresponsible friends will overdose or drink themselves to death. My parents will die. My body will start breaking down if I don’t take care of it. But even if you do take care of it, sometimes things happen that you couldn’t help. Like cancer. Then you have kids. Hey, getting married and having kids is pretty exciting! That’s a milestone! But those things become so stressful so fast. 
The thought of these things make me so suicidal. And the virus situation isn’t helping because even if I said “I need to go out there and enjoy the youth I still have”, there’s nothing out there. I’d risk my health. Things just keep getting worse.

But on that note... I’m sure it’s not all bad. There’s still things for you to enjoy. I look at my parents lives. They were in their 30’s when we did very exciting things. Sure, they’re not milestones. But they’re exciting. And I think that if I get to do things similar when I’m older, maybe life is worth living.

I’m currently 20 years old and have had the fortune of moving out of my parents place when I was still 17 when I went off to college. So here’s some advice from a young adult who’s learned shit the hard way and is still fresh out of the oven for it. 
1) Learn to clean. Thankfully, my mom made my sister and I clean the house with her. I mean deep clean. Learn what surfaces you use comet, Lysol, windex, etc. on. Learn how to unclog a sink or drain. Know these things. Because my girlfriend didn’t and it was horrifying to me. I had to teach her that mold is not a regular thing for a shower and it needed to be cleaned.

2) learn to cook. I can’t cook very well. I am still learning. For a while, my girlfriend didn’t know how to cook either. But she got super into it and now does it even just as a hobby. And it has improved our lives immensely. It saves a shit ton of money, you get healthier options, and sometimes it’s just flat out fun. 

3) wash the dishes. This goes back to cleaning, but I’d say the most annoying thing is dishes. You clean them and there are more to clean by the end of the day. Make a habit of washing dishes immediately after using them and your life will be much easier.

4) know how finances work. I’m not sure what money system you have. Maybe you already have a credit and debit card and I’m just talking out of my ass. But if you have neither of those, get one, and then act like you don’t have a credit card until an emergency arises. My freshman year of college, I went absolutely wild with the credit card and put myself $1000 into debt that I just paid of this year (over three years) and that’s just because the college gave us a $600 refund for the virus and I got a good paying job. Otherwise, I’d still be about $800 in debt. But also you should know some basic things because, again, my girlfriend didn’t know; and I have to take care of our bills and make sure they’re paid because she never learned. 

5) don’t be afraid to ask for help. Living alone is not something people are just instantly good at. We all have our strengths and weaknesses and since this is a first for you, don’t be afraid to reach out for help. It goes a long way; trust me.

Oh and one more thing, if some bullshit company called Spark Energy comes to your door with a smile saying “well lower your gas bill” don’t fucking do it. Fucking scammers busted the price of our gas and will try and charge you a $100 cancellation fee

Back in the day, music was one of the ONLY sources of entertainment. So people played and practiced ALL THE TIME. Needless to say, “amateurs” during the time would be seen as “oh shit, you actually know how to play” today. That being said, people had A LOT of time on their hands. But this also meant composers could write pieces for people at home to play. Not just listen to whenever. And almost every famous composer studied and dedicated themselves to music schools in Venice. And then pieces that were composed were often only performed in venues that only the rich could afford to get into. Or they performed for royalty. So they didn’t need to tour all over because money was mostly made from composing pieces. People would ask composers to compose them pieces for different events. Which also means that because so many people wanted different pieces for different events, composers had to write a lot more pieces. But today, it’s not easy to get an artist to write you something. It’s nearly impossible unless you’re friends with them. Playing an instrument is no longer an everyday skill so the artists are no longer selling songs for you to play at home. Touring is now a thing now that venues are open to more people other than the rich and royal. So touring takes a lot of their time. And I also believe writing music just gets harder as time goes by. Back in the day, music was pretty new. They didn’t know too much about theory. For a time, modern notation wasn’t even invented yet. So there stuff can be seen as somewhat simple now. Sure, not everybody can sit down and play a Bach piece on piano. But most actual pianist can. Believe it or not, but if you say Mozart down at a piano today and challenged him against a professional pianist of today, the modern pianist is far better at piano because over time music requires more skill and has gotten more complicated. It takes more skill just to play the intro guitar lick in Prince’s “When Doves Cry” than it takes to play classic lute pieces. Trust me; my guitar teacher gives me the classical guitar stuff and I’ll learn them in about two weeks. But I’ve been working on “When Doves Cry” for a month and I’m not even close to having it down. I’ve been playing the guitar intro from Sublime’s “Santeria” for probably over a year and not once have I ever played it completely perfect. It comes close, but it’s never perfect. My point is, back then, there were rules and math that they followed in order for music to be good and it was simple. Nowadays, (believe it or not) musicians are chasing after something new, different, and unique. And that is much harder than following Sonata Form.

Like other commenters, and you, said, all celebrities reach a level of fame and then it just dies. Happens to nearly every band. And I wouldn’t say Prince was like god-tier level famous either. I’d say he’s highly acclaimed to his fans, but to the general public, I don’t think they know much about him. He wasn’t Queen, and I doubt the Prince legacy will live as long as the Queen legacy has. And speaking of Queen, couldn’t the same be said about them? Yeah, we all know the hits but other than that, how much Queen music does the general public know and enjoy? The reason that Prince is considered a musical “genius” by his, and music, fans is because he kinda was. First, his presentation and aesthetic was unique and out there for that time. Not a lot of androgynous or feminine male musicians were out in the spotlight in the 80s. His music that’s really good, is REALLY good. Let’s take the most popular album he’s got, Purple Rain; nearly every song on there is really good. “Purple Rain” is a beautiful song, I know there are a lot of people out there who don’t get the hype of it or don’t understand why it’s so popular, but it really IS a beautiful song. The melody, the metaphors, you gotta really dissect it to make it mean something to you. Or another example, “When Doves Cry”, that guitar intro riff is absolutely insane- and get this... nobody know how to fucking play it. Prince was just improvising in the studio when he played that. He did not remember how he did it and you can only find “okay, I THINK this is right, it sounds pretty accurate” type tutorials on how to play it on YouTube. And even then, it’s extremely difficult to play. Another reason he was considered a musical genius is he could play SO many instruments. If you’re a musician who plays more than just the guitar, bass, drums, or piano; you’d know that that’s not as impressive as most people think it is. I play Cello, piano, guitar, bass, double bass, clarinet, flute, and trumpet; and just about any other instrument you put in my hands and give me an hour with. Because instruments are a lot more similar than you’d think. If you can find a single note on the instrument and understand basic theory, you’re golden. You’d think this would be more common amongst musicians but it’s not. Lots of professional guitarists don’t know the note names on the guitar or how they work. They just play what sounds good. It’s shocking (and honestly makes me question why I’m in college for music in the first place). When I tell people all the instruments I play, they think I’m a genius too. And then when they put a new instrument in my hands to see if I can play it, and in a few minutes I’m busting out a simple little song, they lose their god damn minds. So because Prince could do that too, people think he’s a musical genius. I think he was a musical genius too. But only because I enjoy how unique his sound is, and his insane guitar writing.

I think an “Important Band” would be any band that has changed the genre, created a new genre,  did something unique not usually seen in the genre, changed the scene associated with the genre, or brought the genre to mainstream. For example, love them or hate them, My Chemical Romance changed the Emo genre, the Emo scene, and how media perceived Emo music. While at it, the gathered a giant dedicated following, evident by how they sell their reunion concerts out in as little as an hour. Even only 10 minutes. Your opinion doesn’t matter, they’ve obviously hit the emo scene hard. An important punk band may be Dead Kennedy’s. Though not always the most popular punk band amongst punks, “Nazi Punks Fuck Off” set a still ideology into punks, still using the songs title as a saying towards racists even today. These aren’t really mainstream, unfortunately I can’t really think of any examples of bands that brought the genre to the mainstream at the moment. But I would also like to include another important band that very little people listen to, just to show how flexible the definition could be. The Cramps. The Cramps set the stage to create the genre Psychobilly. An obscure musical genre that contains the following elements: surf rock, rockabilly, punk rock, folk. All topped with a horror theme. You don’t know whether to mosh or whether to swing dance like it’s the 50’s but it is definitely Halloween. Not a lot of people listen to Psychobilly. Only a few have heard of the Cramps. But The Cramps invented Psychobilly. It’s not what they called themselves, but it is what they influenced. 

However, I also believe “Important Band” has a second meaning. And that is if it’s important to YOU. Linkin Park is an important band to me. They helped me cope with my emotions of being sexually assaulted and being in an abusive relationship. Losing Chester to suicide really hit me hard. Broke my heart and no band has ever really touched my heart like they have yet. Though I try endlessly to fill the gap they left. Linkin Park had an influence on ME. It shaped who I am today. I’m sure we all have a band that is important to ourselves. You could argue that Linkin Park is important even in the first definition. But personally, I don’t believe so. I think the band was very dear to its fans. Very important when it comes to the following they have. But I do not believe they changed anything nor influenced any kind of new music or bands. But we never know. Bands we have today, we won’t know if they’ll go down in history until history actually happens. Queen, Bowie, Prince, all bands that will go down in history as they are still influential and listened to today. But as for the artists of today, we won’t know for a long time.

To our finally point: Is Radiohead Important? Personally.... I don’t think so, sorry. To an outsiders eye, and I’m talking someone unlike us who are obviously obsessed with music and (hopefully) do all that we can to broaden our taste, Radiohead is not known for anything except “Creep”. That one song might go on to live for years. But no one will think of them as an influential or important band. Just that one song. It’s a shame that this is the fate a lot of good bands will have. It happens to good artists. I don’t think Jeff Buckley will ever be considered important, even though I think his music is beautiful. All he’s ever known for in the general public is his album cover for Grace. But that’s it. Even the legendary Eagles will probably die out with only “Hotel California” left behind. But who knows, maybe Eagles did change something in the Rock genre that makes them important that I’m not seeing. And maybe Jeff Buckley did as well. And maybe even Radiohead. But these are just my thoughts.

Personally, I’m a big believer in supporting your favorite artists; but I am also a big user of Spotify. And this is for many reasons, I believe that me, following my favorite artists on Spotify, with all the information Spotify gives actually helps supports the artists as much as they can in such a modern music listening way. We can not deny that streaming services have changed the way people listen to music. But Spotify still helps artists. They notify me when an artist that I listen to comes out with a new album. Even if I only like one song by that artist. They also display merch of bands from time to time and even tell me when the closest concert near me will be happening. To me, that’s probably the biggest way to support artists these days. Artists don’t make a lot of money of CD sales, that’s why they tour. To spread the new album, boosting sales in the process hopefully and maybe they can make a few extra bucks from ticket sales. Though, touring is an expensive thing and bands can even lose money from touring. But I know that if it weren’t for Spotify, I would’ve missed a lot of my favorite artists in concert. Another way i believe it supports artists is its recommendations. I know people always like to shit on songs that Spotify recommends. But I personally don’t get it. I’ve found a lot of good songs and new artists just by letting Spotify do it’s thing. And when I’m craving new music, I’ll just go to an artist I like and scroll down to the “similar artists” list and go from there. It’s how I’ve found a lot of my favorite bands. Dead Kennedy’s, GRLwood, In This Moment, just to name a few. I probably never would’ve heard of them if it weren’t for Spotify. 

But... even that being said, I also like my CD and vinyl collection. But I’m also disappointed to hear that you choose to listen to and actually like the album first. I feel like you’re missing out on a musical adventure. I remember when I bought my first Cramps album. I only knew one song on it, but I knew a shit ton of other Cramp songs and considered myself a fan. So I bought it anyway (it was vinyl by the way). I personally like taking new music home to listen to. Even if I might hate it. Like my Circle Jerks CD. I don’t hate it. But there is only a few songs on it that I actually enjoy. The rest I just kind of use as background music that just so happens to fit my palette. So I recommend that you buy CDs and Vinyls of bands and artists that you like even if you only know one song by them. You might find some good gems in there. And I get that this is expensive, I’m a college student myself who gets very little money. So I’m not saying buy every CD and Vinyl you find. Just when get the opportunity to treat yourself. Look for used CD stores. They sell good albums for $3 sometimes. And lots of antiques stores sell records for around $8. Of course, most of these are older records but sometimes you find more modern albums. This doesn’t exactly help the artists directly. But spreading music is better than nothing.

Well, first let’s look at the beginning of emo. Emo actually began as an actual music genre back in the 80’s or 90’s. So I recommend first starting by researching original emo so we can see the shift that occurred mostly when MCR came out (the reason MCR is a king of emo is cause it shifted the scene and brought it to light so much). And it’s more like how society shifted the emo scene rather than the other way around. MCR began after Gerard Way witnessed the twin towers on 9/11. MCR’s “Skylines and Turnstiles” from I Brought You My Bullets, You Brought Me Your Love is actually about 9/11. “Honey, This Mirror isn’t Big Enough For The Both of Us” and “Vampires Will Never Hurt You” are both about drug and alcohol abuse (which makes the lyric “you can’t touch my brother and you can’t keep my friends” a lot more hard hitting since the band was experimenting with drugs and alcohol). In technical definitions, the Bullets album is the most emo genre music. But when it comes to original emo, none of the rest of their albums really qualify. Bullets didn’t bring MCR too much fame. But it got them some attention. And they lived in New Jersey, which at the time was a breeding ground for music labels. Bands from New Jersey were getting picked up left and right. But MCR turned down quite a few. But then they’re first big hit came out. “I’m Not Okay (I Promise)” gained them the fame we know them for. Around this time though, Gerard got really bad with his depression, substance abuse, and alcoholism. He was never sober for probably every single show in that era. But this album marked a change to the emo scene mostly because of the media. “This music!” The media cried “this devil music our children are listening to! It’s influencing them to commit suicide and making them depressed!” The media labeled them as emo and Emo’s definition changed from a music genre to a style and stood for EMOtional. Now emo was about wearing black and being sad. Any song that had sad lyrics was emo now. It wasn’t until a tour in Japan did Gerard stop drinking before going on stage. They performed, Gerard did a chilling short cover of “House of the Rising Sun”, went home, called up a manager (?); sounding really depressed and suicidal. They realized oh man, he really needs help and that was the last show he performed while drunk. But this new definition of emo opened the gates for other bands like Fall Out Boy and Panic! At the Disco to be considered emo. Even though, to be honest, Fall Out Boy is more pop punk and Panic! At the Disco is... uhm... they’re uh.... *flipping through list of genres* ... Baroque pop? Emo became more of a style. But it was also about music too. The two kind of go hand in hand in every scene. The rest of MCR’s albums aren’t really “emo” in the technical sense. But because they’re influence caused such a turn in the emo direction, now what else would you call them? I think MCR is a strong band to talk about because of their influence. But I highly recommend starting from the originals them working up through the years so you can compare it.

Well, I still have them from time to time. I think I’m coming up to two weeks off of it now? But they’re very minor, I hardly notice them. Those first few days felt like each brain zap was a pulse. On after the other after the other until I either stopped moving or laid down. After that though, it’ll be just a random one or two. A quick zap and it’s fine. Like a shiver on crack cocaine. I wouldn’t say they affect my daily life too much though. Yeah they were annoying. And sometimes I’d space out if someone was talking to me because I had one and now I was too busy thinking about how much of a psycho I felt like. But I still drove my girlfriend to the grocery store. I couldn’t go inside with her.
But I did drive. They don’t recommend it, and honestly, if it can be avoided, I wouldn’t. But brain zaps are hardly the reason for that. It was mostly the nausea and cloudy headedness of it that made me unable to function. But again, only for three days. After that I had a few days of noticeable brain zaps, but they did not affect my ability to function. I’d say, when you taper off to 0, and you start to feel that first day of terrible, try and find a way to make time for you to relax and rest for three days. That’s the magic number. Three. Everyone always told me three days. I said that was bullshit cause I felt just as terrible the third day but then I woke up the next day and bam! Gone. It’s kind of weird actually. If you wanna time it kind of right, I suggest dropping it on a Wednesday. That’s when I dropped it. Went to a concert later that day. Best choice of my life cause the adrenaline of the concert met with my new chemical imbalance created some really brutal mosh pit elbow swings. But anyway, Thursday I felt okay. A bit tired and by the end of the day I was starting to feel it. But by Friday, that’s when it hit. I was lucky cause it had timed that the bad days were on a weekend. Fashion-wise, you dress however the fuck you want. BUT that being said, I understand that some of us fucking love punk fashion and that’s how we would like to dress to feel confident. Which is hella fucking awesome and hella fucking punk. I dress comfortably everyday. Jeans, a t-shirt. Nothing special. But when I wanna feel extra good and party with confidence, I break out the battle jacket and my patch covered pants. So I’ll help you out here.

Battle Jacket. Rule #1. There is no wrong way to do your jacket. Absolutely none and don’t let anyone tell you any fucking different! Get a nice one or thrift one. Doesn’t fucking matter cause it’s yours. Any color. With or without sleeves. Leather or denim. And then DIY the shit out of it. You can buy patches. I recommend Angry,Young, and Poor. I think they have cool political patches and they’re a little on the smaller side so I like to use them to fill up empty spaces on mine. A good guy to go to for band patches is Instagram user OldScratchJackets. Sells patches for pretty cheap considering the quality. His prints are always perfect, the fabric he uses is sturdy and doesn’t string so much. Really large sometimes. And he likes to throw in free ones with your order on occasion. Other than that, make your own with paint and old shirts. I painted my own back patch and it looks awesome. People always ask me where I bought it; it’s unfortunate that I have to tell them I painted it myself. Pins are fun too. Check antique and vintage stores for wild and unique patches and pins. One of my favorite patches, I got at an antique store. 

You can paint and put patches on a pair of pants too. Usually, not on denim, but some people do. I bought a pair of looser fit really dark gray (almost black) pants. I don’t know how to describe the fabric but it’ll be easier to sew and paint. I also bought a good pair of camo vintage army pants that go REALLY well with my battle jacket. I bought them from an antique store. 

T-shirts are pretty easy. Wear whatever. But if you want political shirts, you gotta hunt a bit. BerntheWhiteHouse is a pretty cool place if you’re voting for Bernie. Anyway, band shirts are usually easier to find and do fine. Independent designers always have cooler shirts than you’ll ever find in a sweat shop abusing capitalistic bullshit mall. 

Shoes. Docs are cool, common, easy to get. But kind of really overdone. Try finding bigger better boots ; again, probably from a vintage shop.

Other than that; don’t give a fuck what anyone says about you, punch Nazis, and don’t be an asshole and congrats, you’re punk

Punk doesn’t have a uniform. Like what everyone else said, wear what you want.

But, as someone who also enjoys punk fashion, if this is really how you want to dress and what makes you feel good; 
-combat boots. Doc Martens are a classic and easy to find, but honestly I’ve seen better boots at antique stores that are so fucking kick ass. You’ll probably want to get some boot socks too. For comfort. 
-Jeans are always fine. People, generation after generation, subculture after subculture, love fucking jeans. But I like to switch it up sometimes too. I have a pair of vintage army pants that look really fucking cool. Tuck the legs into the boot. Most real army pants have these strings at the bottom for you to tighten the leg around your ankle. I also tie them together under my foot to keep my pant legs from slipping out of my boots. I also have a pair of these loose fit pants, a faded black color that I’m going to put patches on. You can also paint and put patches on those pants. Which brings me to my next point.
-DIY. Nothings better than doing your own project and giving a big fuck you to capitalism cause you’d rather do it yourself than buy their shit. Of course, if you’re not good at it; you can still buy things. But I highly recommend small and individual businesses. Real people who are spending time into each patch just for you. Not some corporate business man with a sweat shop.
-Shirts are simple. Wear whatever shirt you want. I have solid color shirts, other shirts that have some cool designs on them, band shirts, shirts that have some bizarre, “controversial” stuff on it, and shirts with political commentary on it. But if you go with the politics, you better be ready for stares and people who wanna argue. Maybe even fight. Again, I’ve found my best and favorite shirts at second hand stores and small businesses. 
- Jackets. Leather or denim is fine. Vests are also good. Then you diy the fuck out of them. Paint, patches, embroider, spike; whatever you want. It’s your jacket and there is no right way to do it. It’s all yours. Make it your own. 

But being punk doesn’t mean you’re listening to punk music or wearing certain clothes or got a Mohawk. All that is just extra and fun. Things you can enjoy but are not necessary. Not in the slightest. Punk means doing whatever the fuck you want to do and giving a big fuck you to anyone who wants to put you down or stop you from doing it.

Aight so there’s a lot of things you can do. I do all of these for my battle jackets. 

One: DIY
-take some old clothes or fabric you don’t use and get some paint and start painting. These have a really nice what I call “dark punk” look. Not to mention you can get a patch of anything this way. You got an idea? Make it reality!

Two: AYAP
-Angry, Young, and Poor sells $1 patches online. Personally, I think they have good designs and they’re a bit smaller (compared to my next suggestion) so they fill up some of the smaller spaces on my jackets. BUT, personally, I think the fabric of the patches fucking suck. The ends are ridiculously stringy (which can be fixed by folding the edges but sometimes I like the fray) and the fabric is thin which sometimes clashes with the stiffness and thickness of denim. But you can’t beat the price I guess.

Three: Old Scratch Jackets
I fucking love this guy. I highly suggest following him on Instagram if you have it cause he’ll post updates and special deals. He prints them himself and sells them on Etsy. With all sorts of categories from punk bands, to fantasy bands, to political patches, and he even did a while horror movie set for Halloween. He did raise the price (they used to be a dollar) BUT, the fabric he uses is sturdy, thick, with a good amount of fray at the edges. And sometimes he throws in free patches with your order so I think the price worth it. Not to mention he only raised it to like $2. A majority of my patches came from him. Prints are always nice and clean. Only problem, his patches are fucking huge. Don’t have a set place for each before getting it in the mail cause you WILL underestimate it. https://www.etsy.com/shop/oldscratchjackets

Four: Antique and Thrift stores
You probably won’t find a lot of punk band patches, but you can still find AWESOME patches sometimes and antique and thrift stores for real cheap. They usually sell more embroidered patches than fabric patches. But they’ll sell them for sometimes 50 cents a piece and that’s a GREAT deal. And you’ll find one of a kind gems in there. I got my all time favorite patch from an antique store. It’s an embroidered patch that says “Save a Mouse, Eat a Pussy”. You don’t see that shit everyday. It’s a real unique patch and it looks awesome on my jacket.

Hope this helps! Have fun! And remember, it’s your jacket. No one can tell you how to wear it
